paragraphs.text: I'm a complete anime beginner. Before Bloom Into You, the only Japanese anime I'd watched was Detective Conan. It's only now sinking in that I started way too high. Hoping to find something to fill the Bloom Into You-shaped hole, I tried several other yuri series in a row, and none quite did it for me :( My copies of Regarding Saeki Sayaka arrived last week, so I immediately started devouring them. Now I'm convinced there really is no substitute for Bloom Into You. The writing is so delicate, and the anime's art is simply gorgeous.

The question my friends ask most is, "Why have you suddenly started watching anime?" To a lot of people, I probably seem pretty set in my ways: I can wear the same Casio watch for ten years, keep a phone for at least five, and fill my bedroom shelves with little things from years ago. But I have my reasons. The watch is a limited edition I bought in Taiwan on a trip after graduating from primary school. I keep the phone because spending all that money to replace it feels like such a waste. And the little things hold so much of my past. When I'm daydreaming in my room, I often drift over to the shelves and look at them. They really can take me back to those precious times I can only revisit in memory: the scent of osmanthus outside after I won the two-dan division of a Go tournament; how itchy I was after lying on the grass for an aerial photograph of our middle-school graduation; a Sunday afternoon long ago, leaning over the balcony railing in the breeze, breathing in the sun-warmed smell of a quilt. I don't want to forget those moments. So I try to keep the memories by keeping the things. They're part of who I was. When I see them, I can see my younger self: small, innocent, carefree, with no idea yet of how the world worked. That's the person I most want to be. I can't quite get back there now, but remembering still brings a warmth to my heart. Surely this is what it means to say, "Home is wherever my heart is at peace."

I've wandered off a bit. The real reason I suddenly started watching anime was that I wanted stories, and a little distance from my own life, to dilute how much real life hurt. I felt weighed down all the time. Classes during the day, then straight to the lab, back to the dorm after ten at night—and only then did I finally get a little time to myself. For a while I tried to take that time back by staying up, scrolling videos and playing games. None of it really helped. So I turned to books and animation. One evening, by chance, I opened a search engine and saw a news story about a Fields medallist's Sayaka mug. That got me curious enough to look up Bloom Into You. The reviews were glowing, so I watched it. Yep. It got me, lol.

Back to the story. Yuu is an absolute angel!!! She's attentive, considerate, gentle, emotionally perceptive—and those might be the least remarkable things about her. Through the early and middle parts of the story, Touko sees being loved as a shackle, a source of pressure. Yuu gives up so, so much to keep her from feeling that pressure. There are things she desperately wants to say but can't, because of Touko's feelings and her own place in the relationship at the time. She accepts Touko's weaknesses and darker sides without conditions, and patiently helps her work through them every time. The perfect girlfriend. An angel, through and through!!!

Touko Nanami. Losing herself, trying so hard to become her sister, being unable to take off that perfect-person mask, running from her feelings—she put my stomach through hell in the early and middle parts. But her performance towards the end was so good that I'm dropping the charges. A kid who learns from her mistakes is a good kid, right? Touko is an incredibly compelling character. That sharp contrast between who she is in public and in private is exactly my thing. But it puts her under so much pressure, too: everyone's picture of her sister, her own idealised memories of her sister, her elders' expectations, her harsh demands on herself… Being able to do anything in public and falling apart in private doesn't tell you everything about her, but it does capture the Touko we see early on. In Fernando Pessoa's Tobacco Shop: “
When I tried to take off the mask, it had already become part of my face.

Ms. Saeki. The one I'm still not over, even if she does get a happy ending. I want to give her my favourite line, one that fits her perfectly: "Love is a hand reaching out, then drawing back." Some call her the most perfectly written losing heroine in anime, manga and games. If all that means is that she doesn't end up with the main character in a contest for love, then yes, she fits the label. But in terms of who she is at heart, how she approaches love, and the whole course of her life, she is nothing like the usual losing heroine. First, there's her confession to Touko during the Kyoto school trip: open, sincere, without hiding. After noticing what's happening between Touko and Yuu, she doesn't run away or give up on herself. She faces it and speaks the love she's kept inside for three years. That takes courage. She isn't confessing to demand a "Be with me" outcome. She's expressing something true. She doesn't force Touko or pressure her into a choice. She just wants an ending to that long, unspoken love where she can put a full stop, good or bad, rather than leave an endless blank. Even after being rejected, she doesn't cling or keep pushing. She remains Touko's close friend, there to support her. She loses the contest, but never her dignity. Second, her personality was never going to let her end up with Touko. Sayaka is capable, intelligent and understanding. She understands Touko almost too well. She knows she can't simply rush to say how she feels because she's in love: Touko needs her beside her as a close friend, not as a girlfriend. At that point, Touko isn't going to have a girlfriend at all. Touko has trapped herself, and Sayaka knows it. Rather than break through that protective shell, she tends to it carefully, looks after Touko, and gives her the strongest support she can. Yuu is different. Yuu is the one who breaks the deadlock. She has a stubborn wish for Touko to stop becoming anyone else and just be herself. Sayaka wants that too, of course, and later the two of them agree on it. But Sayaka's nature means she won't be the one to break that wall. She's the gentle one who watches over her. Finally, and most importantly, Sayaka finds happiness that is entirely her own. In the third volume of Regarding Saeki Sayaka, I think she gets the ending she deserves. She meets Haru. This time she doesn't have to hold herself back. She loves, feels and reaches for what she wants freely, and finally finds happiness. So I don't see her as a losing heroine at all. Quite the opposite: I think she's the most fully realised character in the story. Still, seeing Touko and Sayaka together makes my heart ache for Ms. Saeki. She deserves happiness. She deserves that happy ending!
That's probably enough from me. I'm not much of a writer, so please bear with me.

I made this site to remember a story I love, and the people in it I love: Ms. Saeki, our little angel Yuu, and Nanami-senpai. They were a little light in a dark stretch of my life—like water for someone lost in the desert, ginger soup for a traveller caught in a downpour, medicine for someone who has struggled to get well. I hope that, years from now, opening this page will let me feel the enthusiasm I had then, and the way I could still recognise happiness. Because I know how rare and precious it is, in this world, to stay receptive to love. I don't want to become numb. Maybe, years from now, if this page can bring me even a little comfort or a small smile, that will be the moment this site has done what I made it for.
